title: Chief Robert Pharaoh
summary: Robert Pharaoh was a Montaukett leader whose work connected burial-ground protection, cultural education, community governance, museum development, traditional agriculture, and federal acknowledgment.
content:
Robert Pharaoh was a Montaukett leader who was publicly described as a traditional chief. His work connected burial-ground protection, cultural education, community governance, museum development, traditional agriculture, and the long effort for federal acknowledgment. Sources sometimes spell his surname Pharoah; he should not be confused with other members of the extended Pharaoh family who appear in Montaukett history.1

Defending the North Neck burial ground

In 1989, Robert Pharaoh joined Montaukett families, Shinnecock supporters, singers, and allies at a rally to protect an eighteenth-century burial ground at North Neck. John A. Strong connects the threatened place with Cyrus Charles and records Pharaoh’s participation across a three-generation family presence. The public map keeps this sensitive location broad.2

Governance and community leadership

At a May 3, 1993 community meeting in Riverhead, Robert Pharaoh advanced a hereditary leadership claim. Strong reports that his mother, Montaukett matriarch Olive Pharaoh, endorsed that claim. Other community members supported an elected governance process associated with Robert Cooper. The surviving record documents both models and a real internal debate; it does not require this biography to choose one form of leadership over the other.3

Culture, education, and preservation

Later in May 1993, Pharaoh invited community members and the public to a gathering at Montauk County Park and Indian Fields. Crafts, historical interpretation, and traditional foods made cultural education part of public Montaukett presence. In 1994 he circulated the 1919 James Waters constitution during work to formalize tribal government. In 1996 he established the Friends of the Pharaoh Museum and worked with Terrie Caldwell and Within the Circle on a larger cultural festival. Strong also records an experimental garden near Hog Creek that used traditional agricultural methods.4

Federal acknowledgment work

In spring 1996, Robert Pharaoh filed a letter of intent with the federal acknowledgment office. Consultants then worked for two years on a petition documenting Montaukett history and ninety family genealogies. Community disagreement continued while separate supporters ratified a constitution and elected Robert Cooper as chair in November 1997. Pharaoh disputed that process and warned in 1998 that early casino-development discussions could endanger the acknowledgment work. On June 23, 1998, he submitted the completed Montaukett petition.5

Reading the record carefully

Robert Pharaoh’s biography belongs to a living history of Montaukett sovereignty rather than a simple contest between two individuals. Burial protection, cultural teaching, governance, and acknowledgment were connected forms of community work. Describing the documented disagreement openly preserves that complexity without turning it into a rivalry story or confusing elected and hereditary claims.

References

  • John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island (2001), pp. 162–174.
  • East Hampton Star, February 19, 1998.
why_this_matters: Robert Pharaoh’s work connects preservation, cultural teaching, governance, and federal acknowledgment as related parts of modern Montaukett sovereignty, while preserving the complexity of internal leadership debates.
